q: Why do some people experience deja vu while others never do?
Why do we experience deja vu?
Why do we experience deja vu
Why do some people get deja vu and others don't?
What causes deja vu in some people?
Why do some people experience deja vu more often?
Are some people immune to deja vu?
a: Déjà vu is experienced by approximately 60-80% of people, with the highest frequency among those aged 15-25. The reasons why some people experience it while others never do are not fully understood, but several factors appear to play a role. Age is a significant factor — children under 10 rarely report déjà vu, and the frequency decreases after age 60. Personality traits also matter: people who are more anxious, neurotic, or open to new experiences tend to experience déjà vu more frequently. Memory processing differences may contribute, as those who experience déjà vu often have better memory recall and are more sensitive to spatial and temporal discrepancies. Some research suggests that people with certain neurological conditions like temporal lobe epilepsy experience déjà vu more often, while others with damage to the medial temporal lobe never experience it. Genetic factors may also play a role, as déjà vu tends to run in families. Interestingly, some people report never experiencing déjà vu at all, which may indicate differences in how their brains process familiarity and novelty.

q: What is the psychology of deja vu?
What are the theories of deja vu?
a: Déjà vu, meaning 'already seen' in French, is the phenomenon of feeling like one has lived through the present situation before. It affects 60-80% of people, most commonly those aged 15-25. The main theories include the dual-processing theory (a mismatch between familiarity and recollection), the memory overlap theory (new experiences triggering memories of similar past events), and the attentional theory (lapses in attention causing the brain to misinterpret a scene as familiar). Some people never experience déjà vu, possibly due to differences in memory processing or neural pathway development.
